text: Active Directory organizes every user, computer, and group inside a structure with four levels. In this lesson we'll build that structure from the ground up — domain, tree, forest, and Organizational Unit — and then map a realistic company org chart onto it, so the structure stops being abstract and starts being something you'd actually design.

A domain is the real administrative and security boundary — its own domain controllers, its own copy of the AD database, its own policies. A tree is one or more domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace, like contoso.com and sales.contoso.com. A forest is the outer boundary: one or more trees, connected by trust, sharing a schema and a Global Catalog. Most organizations never need more than a single domain in a single tree in a single forest.

An Organizational Unit, or OU, is a container inside a domain — but unlike a domain, it's not a security boundary, it's an organizational one, and it exists for exactly two reasons. First, applying Group Policy: a GPO linked to an OU only affects what's inside that OU. Second, delegation: you can grant a help desk technician rights to reset passwords for one department's users only, without touching anyone else's account.

Picture Contoso Manufacturing's contoso.com domain. A realistic OU tree gives each department — Sales, IT, HR, Finance — its own OU, and inside each one, users and computers get split into separate sub-OUs. That split isn't cosmetic: a GPO that maps a network drive targets users, while one that enforces a screen-lock timeout targets computers, and splitting them keeps each policy hitting only the right kind of object.

That's the shape every AD environment is built on: forest, tree, domain, and OUs doing the organizing underneath. Next, we'll get into the objects those OUs actually hold — users and groups — and how to manage them both by hand and with PowerShell.
